question: Can an agent turn a compute request into the right offer across two clouds, and where does it add something the deterministic matcher cannot?
summary: The agent only adds value where the request is incomplete or the ranking misses the workload, and without a gold standard we cannot yet say how often it is right.

findings.title: There is no gold standard yet
findings.text: Every verdict here compares the agent with the matcher. Agreement shows the two are consistent, not that either is right. We need requests with answers fixed in advance before we can measure correctness.

findings.title: On a complete jobspec the agent explains but does not decide
findings.text: On the four plain requests every run picked the matcher's first answer. The agent added a short explanation for about 20 cents and half a minute. A complete jobspec needs only the matcher.

findings.title: The agent did better when the ranking ignored the workload
findings.text: For the tightly coupled MPI job the matcher chose an exact fit. Every agent run chose hpc7g instead, which costs less in total and has an RDMA network. The ranking should learn this, or the agent stays for such cases.

findings.title: Repeatable answers can still be wrong
findings.text: The first batch gave the same answer on every repeat, and many answers were wrong because the match tool saw only part of the database. The agent reasoned well from bad data and invented a cause for the impossible request.

findings.title: Better tools fixed what prompts would not
findings.text: Once the match tool explained an empty result itself, all six impossible runs named the real cause, the quota, and cost half as much. Nothing in the prompt changed.

findings.title: Requests leave out what users care about
findings.text: The cheapest answers are now mostly Arm or burstable machines. No request says which CPU it needs, so a user with x86 code would get a machine that cannot run it.

findings.title: Flexible mode went untested
findings.text: It matched strict mode on every run because no request needed reshaping. The set needs a request whose shape fails while its totals fit.

findings.title: AWS winning reflects our accounts
findings.text: Google's quota here allows one node per placement group for most types, and each cloud has one region. A fair cross-cloud comparison needs similar quotas and more regions.

next: Build a gold standard first. Then add CPU architecture to the request, add requests that only flexible mode can place, and hand the pick to the secretary to try the allocation.

hypotheses.claim: For a request that fits, the agent picks the matcher's first offer, or one in its top ten for a reason the ranking does not weigh.
hypotheses.text: Every plain request matched the first offer. Every MPI run chose from the top ten for its RDMA network.

hypotheses.claim: The agent's jobspec never asks for less than the user did, and from words alone it keeps every stated constraint.
hypotheses.text: The code refuses weaker requests, and the words were read the same way every time. But the words never state a CPU architecture, so a faithful reading still picks Arm.

hypotheses.claim: When nothing fits, the agent says so and never shrinks the request.
hypotheses.text: It never shrank the request. It gave the right cause only once the match tool reported it.

hypotheses.claim: A request costs cents, not dollars.
hypotheses.text: A run cost 20 cents on average and 33 at most on Bedrock with Claude Opus 5.
